paper_title: StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.

Introduction Interactive video world models shift video generation from producing clips for passive viewing to synthesizing environments that respond to user commands [13, 18, 28, 38, 39, 41, 45, 54, 64]. Systems such as Genie 3 [6, 33, 34, 45] build controllable generative worlds on demand, aiming to offer new form of interactive entertainment. For the generated content to constitute world rather than sequence of individually plausible frames, it must first preserve its 3D structure, without deformation, as the viewpoint changes. At the same time, usable interaction requires the model to give stable feedback to user commands. Basic operations such as moving and turning the camera should have consistent and predictable effect throughout the interaction. Evaluating whether an interactive world model meets these requirements takes more than measuring the perceptual quality targeted by conventional video benchmarks [21, 22, 31]. Recent benchmarks have therefore begun to assess such models along two axes, spatial consistency and action control. To assess 3D structure, metrics such as those of WBench and MEt3R [2, 56, 58, 61] reconstruct the scene from the generated frames with 3D foundation models such as VGGT [47] and Depth Anything 3 [30]. They then check whether the frames are consistent with this reconstruction. This geometric reference, however, is fitted to the video under test. Since such foundation models can fit seemingly coherent geometry even to inconsistent images [35], gradual scene deformation can be absorbed into the reference and go undetected by these benchmarks. For action control, the reference raises the same issue. Benchmarks such as WorldScore and WBench [9, 58, 61] compare the recovered camera trajectory with the commanded one after aligning their scales, which accommodates models with different control interfaces. This scale is likewise estimated from the trajectory under test, so it averages out changes in the distance per command. model whose steps lengthen or shorten midway can therefore still match the commanded path. Loop-closure tests [14, 25, 29, 51, 55, 56, 59] avoid rescaling but typically assume that opposite commands cancel, an assumption that many current models violate, as shown in App. H.3. They also test whether loop returns to its start rather than whether each command keeps stable effect along an open route. How to test scene geometry and action control against references independent of the video under test therefore remains open. To this end, we introduce StrideWorld, benchmark for scene rigidity and action consistency. Each of its references is fixed before the motion it judges, as shown in Fig. 1. The Rigidity test places 3D anchors at the ground-truth depth of each start view and checks whether the visible surfaces stay in place as the camera moves. For actions, we measure the stride of each action from the models own first four steps, so models with different interfaces need no shared unit of motion. The stride is the camera motion of one command, and it predicts the camera pose at every later step. The Pace test checks whether the camera keeps this stride when single action is held, and the Composition test checks whether the strides add up along multi-action routes. These routes come in pairs designed to reach the same end, for example the same translations in different order. Each route is compared with its own prediction and with its partner. The camera is recovered at every step, which locates where route stalls or drifts from its prediction. We evaluate fifteen open models on 54,600 videos generated from 140 start views across 30 scenes, as shown in Fig. 2. All models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves. How well model preserves the scene does not predict how well it composes actions. When single action is held, most models move in the commanded direction and keep steady pace. When actions are combined into routes, however, several models often stall partway. Even completed routes mostly end away from the positions predicted by the models own strides. Part of this error arises at action switches, where models carry the previous action over or start the new one slowly. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to their predictions. Existing metrics largely miss these failures, as reconstruction-based reprojection error detects scene deformation in only three of the fifteen models. When the pace of rendered video grows by half, scale-fitted trajectory error flags 43% of such videos, whereas the Pace test flags 94% at the same false-alarm rate. Finally, fine-tuning two models on 112 rendered clips with exact camera paths removes most of their mid-route stalls and more than doubles their Composition scores. In summary, our contributions are as follows: 1. We propose StrideWorld, which measures scene rigid2 ity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view and action consistency against each models own action strides. We validate its measurements on rendered videos with known camera motion and its scores against the judgments of ten human raters. 2. We benchmark fifteen open interactive video world models and find that most deform their scenes as the camera moves. They keep steady pace under single action but often fail when actions are combined into routes. 3. We show that fine-tuning two models on 112 rendered clips with exact camera paths removes most of their midroute stalls and brings route endpoints closer to their predictions without lowering image-quality scores. 2. Related Work Interactive video world models. World models were first studied in reinforcement learning as learned simulators of an agents environment [15, 16]. Building on video generation models trained at scale [1, 5, 46, 57], camera-controlled video models condition an entire clip on prescribed camera trajectory [17, 65], whereas 3D world generators lift generated content into explicit 3D scenes [38, 42, 44]. Interactive video world models instead generate each new segment in response to user commands [6, 28, 33, 45, 64], given as discrete keys [18, 39, 41, 49, 66], camera poses [13, 20, 36, 38, 40, 44, 60, 62], or text prompts [7]. To keep the scene stable over long interactions, recent models maintain memory of past frames, patches, or implicit 3D features [36, 39, 49, 54, 62], condition on an explicit 3D cache [38], encode camera geometry in their positional embeddings [53], or use reinforcement learning to reduce long-horizon drift [14, 50]. Their control interfaces express motion in different units, from key presses of unspecified length to camera displacements normalized by scene depth. The same command therefore moves the camera by different amounts across models. Evaluating action control. Early video benchmarks assessed perceptual quality, physical plausibility, and instruction following [3, 4, 21, 22, 27, 31]. Interactive benchmarks add action control and use different motion references, as listed in Tab. 1. Direction metrics check the commanded motion axis [56, 63], and WorldMark also measures heldcommand speed decay in optical flow. Trajectory metrics compare the recovered camera path with reference after scale alignment or normalization [8, 9, 11, 58, 59, 61], so their sensitivity to pace depends on the reference and the temporal alignment. WorldRoamBench [55] builds an adaptive reference from each predicted segments displacement and compares paths at matched arc length. Similarly, groupaction tests [51] check identity, inverse, and composition relations, and WorldCycle [14] evaluates endpoint closure, mirrored forwardreverse frames, and phase-aligned repeated cycles. StrideWorld instead uses separately calibrated strides to measure each step on open routes, without fitting the routes scale or requiring opposite actions to cancel, since each action has its own stride. Evaluating geometric consistency. Evaluating 3D consistency hinges on what serves as the geometric reference, which Tab. 1 also lists. Most benchmarks derive this reference from the generated video itself. Like MEt3R [2] for generated images, they reconstruct the scene and camera from the generated frames with SLAM or 3D foundation models and measure how well the views agree with this reconstruction [9, 32, 48, 52, 56, 58, 61]. This approach needs no external 3D reference, but the reference is fitted to the generated frames. Because 3D foundation models can fit seemingly consistent geometry even to inconsistent images [35], gradual deformation can be absorbed into the reference. Other benchmarks compare generated views with ground truth rendered by game engine or simulator [19, 55, 59] or with registered RGB-D captures [32]. Such references constrain the available viewpoints, and control errors can enter the comparison when the generated and reference viewpoints differ. Orbia also evaluates self-consistency at recovered cameras and renders held-out generated views from reconstructed Gaussian scene [32]. StrideWorld instead takes ground-truth depth only from the start view and evaluates rigidity at the recovered camera, using disjoint anchors for pose fitting and testing. 3 ferent actions. The routes form four pairs, and the two routes of each pair are designed to end at the same place under ideal actions. In the cancel pair, the two routes insert back-and-forth detours of equal length along different axes into shared base path, schematically WADW versus WWSW. The three swap pairs execute the same translations in different orders, either directly (WWD vs. DWW), after turn (YRWD vs. YRDW), or across turns. All sequences are kept short enough for the surfaces of the start view to remain visible, so that the camera can be recovered from ground-truth geometry throughout. Long-horizon exploration and revisits are therefore outside the scope of StrideWorld. In total, each model generates 3,640 videos (2,520 single-action and 1,120 route videos), for 54,600 videos across all models. Models and interfaces. We evaluate fifteen open models covering three control interfaces. Five are driven by discrete keys or tokens (Matrix-Game 2.0 and 3.0 [18, 49], SANAWM [66], DreamX-World [41], and HY-World 1.5 [39]), nine by camera poses (Matrix-Game 3.5 [36], HY-World 2.0 [44], LingBot-World v2 [13], AlayaWorld [40], Lyra 2.0 [38], EVOKE [60], WorldCrafter [62], SolarWM [20], and HY-WorldPlay [39]), and one by text prompts (H3World [7]). Each model runs its released inference configuration, and thin adapter maps the six actions to its native interface. As shown in Fig. 2b, single step moves the camera by widely different amounts across models, and the interfaces share no unit of motion. Because our tests measure motion in each models own strides, command magnitudes need not match across models. We therefore use models default per-step command when its motion is clearly measurable and keeps the start-view surfaces visible over 16 held steps, and otherwise set fixed magnitude that does. All command magnitudes are released with the benchmark, as detailed in App. and H.6. 4. Evaluation Protocol StrideWorld tests scene rigidity, single-action pace, and multi-action composition. Every model deviates 1.6 to 7.3 times more than its rigid counterpart, as shown in Fig. 3a, so tracking noise alone does not account for the excess. This excess has two possible sources, scene that deforms over time and scene that stays rigid at wrong 6 depth. Refitting the depth of each held-out anchor and the camera freely removes the second. The ratio of Lyra 2.0 then falls to one, whereas the other fourteen models stay at 1.2 or above, so the excess of Lyra 2.0 comes mostly from fixed depth error. It conditions each new view on an explicit 3D cache built from estimated depth [38], so the surfaces it has already shown keep the same geometry, which suggests that 3D representation mitigates deformation. Preserving the scene does not make model follow commands. The Rigidity ranking of the models shows no relation to their Composition score ranking, with Spearman correlations of 0.01 for the offset and 0.07 for the counterpart ratio (App. G.3 and D.1). 5.2. Held actions keep steady pace When single action is held for 16 steps, most models move in the commanded direction and keep the pace set by their first four steps. Twelve of the fourteen ranked models have median pace ratio within the steady band of 0.8 to 1.25, as shown in Fig. 3b, and the text-driven H3-World is only slightly faster. The same pattern holds with equally weighted strides (App. E.2). Among the ranked models, only DreamX-World changes pace strongly. It accelerates over the first steps of hold, so its first four steps no longer predict where held command leads. AlayaWorld moves slowly during its first steps, which makes its stride hard to measure, and its stride-based metrics are therefore shown in grey, left unranked, and marked by in Tab. 2 (App. E). 5.3. Composed routes stall and drift Once actions are combined into routes, the strides of most models no longer predict where their routes end, as shown in Fig. 3c. Only HY-World 2.0 and Lyra 2.0 bring more than three quarters of their routes within one stride of the predicted endpoint, whereas most other models do so for fewer than quarter. Both take camera poses as input and scale translations by the estimated depth of the start view, so the same command moves the camera by consistent fraction of the scene. Tying commands to scene depth thus appears to help strides add up along route. The interface alone does not explain this gap, as Near ranges from 3.1% to 84.3% across the ranked camera-pose models and the key-driven Matrix-Game 3.0 outperforms all of them except HY-World 2.0 and Lyra 2.0. The routes of the other models fail in two main ways, illustrated in Fig. 4. The first is mid-route stalls, where the camera stops for step partway through route, most often when new action starts. Stalls affect more than third of the routes in four ranked models, as listed in Tab. 2, and account for most incomplete routes. The second is endpoint drift, where even completed routes end well away from their prediction. The median error is above one stride in eleven of the fourteen ranked models. In four ranked models, the same actions in different order end about two to three times farther apart than repeated generation predicts. Regenerating the routes with two further seeds shows that this drift is systematic, as routes end error is median 1.8 to 3.7 times the spread of its ends across seeds. Part of the error arises at action switches, where some models carry the previous action over and others start the new action with only about half stride, whereas the leading models keep the same step before and after the switch (App. F). Existing control metrics miss much of this, as direction checks miss both failure modes and direction accuracy shows no clear relation to models Composition score. trajectory error with fitted scale also misses many failed routes, even when it is given the stride-predicted path as its reference. After fitting one scale, about fifth of the stalled routes still have an error below 10% of the path, and so do about quarter of the routes that end more than two strides from their prediction. The error also does not show where along route the failure occurs (App. F.7). 5.4. Measurements are accurate and robust On videos rendered in UE5 along known camera paths, the recovered cameras deviate from the true ones by median of 1.5% in translation and 0.3% in rotation. Adding blur, compression, flicker, or moderate wobble keeps these median errors within 4.0% and 2.1%. On the generated videos, other calibration lengths, stall thresholds, and camera-recovery anchors leave all findings unchanged, and the route findings hold when the commands of three models are halved or doubled (App. G, H, and A.4). We then change one property of rendered video by known amount to test whether each metric responds to the failure it targets, as shown in Fig. 5. Deformation injected into the rigid counterparts raises the Rigidity offset linearly, while texture drift, flicker, and occluders leave it near its level on the rigid counterparts. The reprojection error of feed-forward reconstruction, by contrast, responds to texture drift and to blur with compression at least as strongly as to deformation. On the generated videos, it separates only three of the fifteen models from their rigid counterparts, whereas the Rigidity offset separates all fifteen. On the action side, Fig. 5a applies every test at its default threshold. When each test is instead set to flag 5% of the ideal held videos, the Pace test flags 94% of the held videos whose pace grows to 1.5 times. scale-fitted trajectory error flags only 43% of them, because its scale absorbs part of the change. Scene deformation also shifts the recovered camera, which at the level seen in generated videos changes the Near decision of 8% to 20% of routes but leaves the model ranking unchanged (App. G.4). (b) Median change of the Rigidity offset (blue) and of the VGGT reprojection error (grey) against the rigid counterpart, as share of the change at 2 of smooth deformation, with 95% bootstrap intervals. Flag rules and settings are given in App. G.4. author raters blind to the models and metrics. They rated 160 randomly sampled videos for whether the camera follows the commands, with Fleiss κ of 0.87, and the score of each video separates those judged good with an AUC of 0.88. On 140 completed swap pairs, the pair score separates those judged to end at the same place with an AUC of 0.83, against at most 0.74 for scores with fitted scale. For two videos of the same route whose Rigidity offsets differ at least twofold, the majority of raters chose the one with the smaller offset as more stable in all 39 untied pairs (App. I). 6. Fine-Tuning on Rendered Camera Paths Along composed routes, several models often stall and most completed routes end away from their predictions, as shown in Sec. 5.3. Since every command step in rendered clip moves the camera by an exact displacement or turn, we test whether fine-tuning on few such clips reduces these failures. We render 112 training clips in procedural Blender scenes that share no assets or routes with StrideWorld, and fine-tune LoRA adapters on the non-distilled base models of HY-World 1.5 and SANA-WM. On the full benchmark of 3,640 videos, both fine-tuned models improve over their base models on every consistency metric without lowering image-quality scores. Stalled routes fall from 72.0% to 11.2% for HY-World 1.5 and from 57.9% to 23.1% for SANA-WM. The Composition score of both models more than doubles and exceeds that of the released models in Tab. 2, and the Rigidity offset also falls, by about two fifths for SANA-WM. For HY-World 1.5, we further examine what these gains depend on. They hold on the real ETH3D views although all training clips are rendered. We then randomly perturb the step lengths of the training clips, so that every command step still moves the camera but by varying amount. Fine-tuning on these clips retains about four fifths of the stall reduction, and exact step lengths add the rest. Tab. J.1 and App. give the full results. 7. Conclusion StrideWorld tests interactive video world models against references that are fixed before the motion they judge. It compares the scene with the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and each action with the stride set by the models own first steps. Across fifteen open models, nearly all deform their scenes as the camera moves. Most keep steady pace under single held action, but their composed routes often stall partway or end away from the positions predicted by their own strides. Two design choices stand out among the stronger models. The one that conditions on an explicit 3D cache preserves the scene best, and the two that scale commands by the estimated scene depth compose routes best. Fine-tuning two models on few rendered clips with exact camera paths also removes most of their mid-route stalls. Extending StrideWorld to dynamic scenes and full 6-DoF trajectories is natural next step (App. M).

sections.title: G Validation on Known Motion and Rigid Renderings
sections.content: G.1 Pose recovery on known motion We first recover the cameras of 30 segments from ten UE5 sequences with exact camera trajectories recorded by the engine, placing anchors on the first frame with the sampler of the benchmark (App. B.1), which gives median of 403 anchors per segment. All 30 segments are solved, with median 2D tracking error of 0.117% of the image diagonal (90th percentile, P90, 0.176%). After the ray-space refinement, the recovered cameras deviate from the true ones by median of 1.48% in translation and 0.31% in rotation (P90 3.98% and 0.68%), against 2.28% and 0.46% after EPnP with RANSAC alone. We then apply synthetic degradations to all frames after the first, and as shown in Tab. G.1, all 390 degraded segments are solved and pass the pose checks. Blur, compression, and flicker change the median pose errors by at most 0.12 percentage points, and moderate wobble of 0.5% of the diagonal, alone or combined with the other degradations, keeps the median translation and rotation errors within 3.98% and 2.09%. Only the strongest wobble of 1% raises them to 8.26% and 4.40%. Table G.1. Pose recovery on the 30 ground-truth segments under synthetic degradations (median / P90, in percent). We also pass the true and the recovered cameras of five groups of rendered UE5 control videos, each with six eight-step single actions and two composed routes, through stride calibration and scoring. Pace score differs by 1.2 points (98.8 vs. 100.0), Pair by 0.7 points in position and 1.8 points in heading, and single-route scores by at most 3.3 points, so camera recovery leaves the scores nearly unchanged. G.3 Rigid floor and rigid counterparts We render 417 rigid videos of three procedural layouts along the six held actions and eight routes of the benchmark at 832 480, 24 fps, and H.264 (CRF 23), with translation strides from 1% to 16% of the start views median depth and turns of 1 to 6 per step. Scored by the unchanged pipeline, their median Rigidity offset over frames with 28 of image motion is 0.13 (12,660 frames from 389 videos) and stays between 0.10 and 0.15 across all six motion settings. With per-frame medians in place of per-frame means, the floor is 0.08, which Lyra 2.0 matches, while SolarWM lies 1.6 above Lyra and the other thirteen models lie 2.4 to 3.8 above it, as shown in Tab. D.1. Since resolution, frame rate, step duration, compression, and camera path all affect tracking noise, we also build the rigid counterpart of Sec. 5.1 for each of the 20 route videos of every model that have the most frames in 28 of image motion. The start view and its ground-truth depth are triangulated into mesh split at depth discontinuities and rendered along the camera path recovered from the generated video, at the models resolution, frame rate, length, codec, and bitrate. As shown in Tab. G.2, every model exceeds its rigid counterpart on the same frames, with 95% bootstrap intervals of the ratio entirely above 1.0. The ratio is 2.1 to 7.3 for twelve models and 1.6 for Lyra 2.0, SolarWM, and H3-World. The offsets of 32 the counterparts themselves range from 0.054 to 0.167, because the selected videos differ in camera path, image motion, and content even between models of the same format, so the ratio and the absolute offset of Tab. 2 order the ranked models differently (Spearmans ρ = 0.67). HY-World 1.5, for example, has an absolute offset in the middle of the models but the largest ratio, as its counterparts have the smallest offset, and Tab. 2 therefore reports both. Since the held-out anchors lie at the ground-truth depth of the start view, rigid scene generated with wrong depth would also exceed its counterpart. On the same 20 videos of every model and on their counterparts, we therefore fit the depth of each held-out anchor freely along its viewing ray in the start view, over 121 log-spaced values from 0.2 to 5 times its ground-truth depth, to minimize the mean offset of the anchor over all later frames, and score each video with these depths on its frames with 28 of image motion. Freeing the depth lowers the offsets of the generated videos to median of 45% to 77% of their values at ground-truth depth across models and those of the counterparts to 42% to 74%, so both shrink by similar fractions. For fourteen models the generated videos still exceed their counterparts by 1.5 (SolarWM) to 9.5 (HY-World 1.5), with 95% intervals entirely above 1.0 (Free depth in Tab. G.2), so their excess offset is not explained by rigid scene of wrong depth and reflects deformation as the camera moves. We also fit the camera of every frame and focal-length scale of every video between 0.7 and 1.4 jointly with these depths, to the pose and held-out anchors together, on generated videos and counterparts alike. The ratio then shrinks but stays above one for the same fourteen models, from 1.2 (SolarWM) to 4.3 (HY-World 1.5), again with intervals entirely above 1.0. For Lyra 2.0 the ratio falls to 1.2 under free depth and to 0.9 under the joint fit, with intervals that include 1.0, so most of its small excess comes from depth error that stays fixed as the camera moves, as expected when every view is conditioned on 3D cache built from estimated depth. We further inject smooth low-frequency 3D displacement fields, six spatial Fourier modes growing linearly over time, into the counterpart meshes of Lyra 2.0, Matrix-Game 3.0, and SolarWM at amplitudes that move the held-out anchors by 0.25, 0.5, 1, and 2. In all three formats the Rigidity offset grows linearly with the injected deformation, with slopes of 0.59, 0.69, and 0.62. The slopes stay below one because the camera fitted to the pose anchors absorbs part of any smooth surface deformation. Refitting per-video focal-length scale on the pose anchors for eight models gives scales between 0.72 and 1.16 and changes the Rigidity offset by only 5% to +2% (Focal in Tab. Calibrating strides on the first 2, 6, or 8 steps instead of four changes Composition score by at most 1.8 points for every model, while longer windows predict held actions slightly better because they observe more of the 16-step hold. Setting the stall threshold to 0.05 or 0.15 instead of 0.10 changes the number of completed pairs by at most 10 of 560 for the leading models and changes the scores of completed pairs by at most 2.1 points for thirteen models, preserving the separation between models. Halving or doubling the stride units bt and br reverses the order of at most two of the 105 model pairs. Predicting routes from idealized axis-aligned strides instead of the full planar strides Ua SE(2) changes composition scores by at most 5.8 points in position and 2.8 points in heading. Removing the stall check adds back exactly the routes counted as stalled in Tab. 2, confirming that the check filters only stalls. H.3 Opposite actions do not cancel Loop-closure tests assume that opposite commands cancel, but calibrating strides on each action shows that they generally do not. On the cancel pairs (G1), the calibrated strides predict nonzero offset between the two routes, and scoring against these predictions gives lower composition scores than assuming exact cancellation for thirteen models, by up to 22.6 points in position for LingBot-World v2. This offset is consistent across seeds, as the predicted offset between the two routes exceeds twice its standard error across the three seeds for 56% to 94% of the cancel pairs in fourteen models, at least three times the rate expected for zero offset, and only H3-World stays near chance. On the swap pairs (G2G4), where both routes execute the same actions in different orders, the two predictions differ by at most 0.2 points. 37 H.4 Model-wide stride references Models share no common unit of motion, and their median translation strides span factor of 80 and their forward strides alone factor of 139, as shown in Fig. 2b. Three camera-pose interfaces also tie the length of commanded translation to the scene. HY-World 2.0 sets the median depth of the start view to one, Lyra 2.0 scales trajectories by its monocular depth estimate, and LingBot-World v2 normalizes each trajectory by its largest step. Calibrating stride on each videos first steps gives every model its own unit. Replacing it with single stride per model and action, taken as the median across all videos, lowers Pace score for fourteen models because each video is then penalized for variation across views and scenes as well, but the model order stays largely the same (Spearman ρ = 0.95), with Lyra 2.0 first and AlayaWorld and H3-World last under both references. sections.title: I Human Study
sections.content: Ten paid research assistants who are not authors rated generated videos through web interface, blind to the models and the metric scores. All of them gave informed consent before taking part, and each rater worked independently on all three parts of the study. The commanded actions were shown beneath every video with the active step highlighted, playback stopped at the final evaluated step, and an answer could be submitted only after the full clip had played once. Questions. For single videos (Part A), raters answered Overall, does the camera move stably according to the commands? rating of Good means that every step moves in the commanded direction at roughly steady pace without sudden acceleration, slowdown, stalling, jumping, or drift off course, and raters were instructed to judge camera motion independently of visual quality or surface deformation. For swap pairs (Part B), the two route videos were played side by side and their final frames were then shown enlarged next to each other. Raters judged whether the two routes end at the same place by comparing the position and size of fixed objects such as corners, doors, and pillars in the two final frames. They counted them as the same place when these objects nearly coincide, with an offset of at most about 3% of the image width, and as different places when the camera has visibly moved forward, backward, or sideways or turned, or when unsure. For rigidity pairs (Part C), two videos generated by different models from the same start view along the same route were played side by side, and raters chose the video in which the scene keeps its shape more stably, following few fixed objects such as doors, window frames, and furniture in both videos and ignoring sharpness, color, lighting, image quality, and whether the camera follows the commands. Parts and were preceded by worked examples, and both are forced choices. Their instructions were refined after pilot sessions with the first raters, and all ten raters completed both parts under the final instructions. Items and scores. Part covers 160 randomly sampled videos from fifteen models, 80 with single held action and 80 with composed route, plus 10 repeated videos. The three raters of the earlier rounds rated only the 50 videos that are new in this round, and their earlier ratings of the remaining 110 videos are reused. Each single-action video is scored by its Pace score and each route video by its route score sq of App. C.2, which is zero for incomplete routes. Part covers 140 G2G4 swap pairs in which both routes are completed, ten from each of fourteen models spread evenly over that models range of pair scores sp, plus 10 repeated pairs, and each pair is scored by its pair score. Part covers 40 pairs, each scored by the per-video Rigidity offset with the frame selection of Tab. 2. Both videos of pair have at least eight evaluated frames and similar amount of camera motion, with their numbers of evaluated frames and their median image motion within factor of 1.5. In 32 strong pairs the larger offset is at least four times the smaller and at least 0.8, and in 8 moderate pairs it is two to three times the smaller and at least 0.5. Six strong pairs are repeated with the sides swapped. Analysis. The analysis was fixed before any answer was collected. The label of an item is the choice of at least six of the ten raters, and items split five to five are excluded. In Parts and B, item-level agreement is the ROC AUC of the score for the majority label, with 95% bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples of start views within models, and model-level agreement is Spearmans ρ between the share of positive ratings and the mean score, resampled over models. In Part C, agreement is the share of pairs whose majority chose the video with the smaller offset, tested against chance with binomial test. Individual choices are further modeled by logistic regression on the log offset ratio, with standard errors clustered by rater, and the difference in MUSIQ quality [24] between the two videos is added as covariate to test whether raters followed image quality instead of scene shape. Results. As shown in Tab. I.2 and Fig. I.1, raters agree closely with one another and with the scores. In Part A, Fleiss κ is 0.87, mean pairwise agreement is 95%, and 81 of 82 repeated judgments are identical. The per-video score separates the 113 of 160 videos judged good with an AUC of 0.88 [0.82, 0.93], which is 0.87 on single-action and 0.85 on route videos. The majority judged 17 of the 18 stalled routes as bad, and these routes score zero. Completion alone, used as binary score, separates the route videos judged good with an AUC of 0.75 [0.67, 0.82], and the route score raises this by 0.10 [0.04, 0.16] under the same resampling, so the distance between the end of route and its prediction carries information that raters perceive beyond completion. On the 62 completed routes alone, where 46 are judged good and 16 bad, the AUC of the route score is 0.71 [0.57, 0.84], because single video does not show the stride-predicted endpoint and raters in Part instead judge whether the camera moves steadily along the way. Across models, the share of positive judgments follows the mean score with ρ = 0.77 [0.35, 0.96]. In Part B, Fleiss κ is 0.83, pairwise agreement is 92%, and 95 of 100 repeated judgments are identical. The majority judged 62 pairs to end at the same place and 77 at different places, with one tie, and the pair score separates the two groups with an AUC of 0.83 [0.76, 0.89]. Both routes of every pair are completed and their final frames are shown side by side, so this AUC is measured on completed routes in setting where raters compare the two ends directly. In Part C, the majority chose the video with the smaller Rigidity offset in all 31 strong pairs that had majority (p < 109, one pair tied) and in all 8 moderate pairs (p = 0.008). Individual raters agreed with the offset in 87.5% to 100% of the pairs (median 95%), Fleiss κ is 0.86, and 56 of 60 repeated judgments chose the same video after the sides were swapped. Because the pairs were selected for at least twofold difference in offset and nearly every pair is answered in line with the offset, Part tests whether raters perceive clear differences in offset, and the logistic slope on the offset ratio is close to zero within this sampled range. The chosen video had the higher MUSIQ score in 60% of the choices, and with the quality difference as covariate the model still predicts that raters choose the video with the smaller offset in 95% of the choices when the two videos are of equal quality (intercept 3.02 [1.25, 4.79]). Comparison with other scores. The majority labels of Part also allow comparison with other control scores. Direction accuracy is the share of steps that move along the commanded axis or turn the commanded way. The trajectory errors are the root mean square position error over the step boundaries divided by the length of the predicted path, as in App. F.7, either after fitting one scale or similarity transform, or with the scale fixed to the calibrated strides. The per-step error is the mean distance between the displacement of each step and that of its stride, in strides, again without any fit. All trajectory errors use the stride-predicted path as their reference, which existing benchmarks do not have for key-driven models. As shown in Tab. I.1, over the 149 videos on which every score is defined, the StrideWorld scores reach an AUC of 0.88, against 0.53 to 0.71 for the other scores, and the difference to each of them has 95% bootstrap interval above zero. Most of this gap comes from held actions (0.86 against 0.40 to 0.69), although with 70 held videos the interval of the difference includes zero for the trajectory errors with fitted and with fixed scale. On route videos, all scores that use the stride-predicted path agree with the raters to similar degree (0.78 to 0.84), and direction accuracy reaches 0.72. On completed routes, the scores that follow the whole route agree better (0.77 to 0.85, including 0.82 for the per-step error) than the route score, which measures the end error (0.71), as raters judge whether the camera moves steadily along the way. For this reason, StrideWorld reports per-step diagnostics such as stalls, carry-over, and slow starts alongside the Composition score. The majority labels of Part allow the same comparison on swap pairs, where every other score is averaged over the two routes of pair. Over the 139 pairs with majority label, the pair score reaches an AUC of 0.83, against 0.66 to 0.71 for the other scores (last row of Tab. I.1), and the difference to each of them has 95% bootstrap interval above zero, with 0.15 [0.06, 0.23] for the trajectory error with fitted scale and 0.16 [0.08, 0.23] with similarity transform. Taking the worse of the two routes instead of their mean changes no value by more than 0.02. Because raters in Part compare the two ends, we also score each pair by how far the offset between the ends of its two routes departs from the offset between their predicted ends, as share of the path length. With the scale fixed to the calibrated strides, this end offset is the position part of the pair score up to its normalization, and it agrees with the raters equally well (0.84). Fitting one scale to each route lowers its AUC to 0.74, drop of 0.10 [0.04, 0.15], and fitting similarity transform lowers it to 0.68, so reference fitted to each video removes part of the difference between the two ends that raters see. sections.title: K Reproducibility and Supplementary Video
sections.content: StrideWorld is built on synthetic scenes rendered in Unreal Engine 5 and real scenes from ETH3D. We will release all 140 start views with ground-truth RGB images, depth maps, and camera parameters, together with the model adapters and input command sequences for all fifteen models, the evaluation and scoring code, and the recovered camera trajectories and scores of all 54,600 generated videos. Start-view preprocessing and control settings are given in App. A, and pose recovery and scoring in App. and C. The supplementary video (StrideWorld supp video.mp4, 64 s) shows the measurements of the three tests of Fig. 1 on generated videos, each for two models on the same start view and commands, with step-synchronized command overlays. For Rigidity it overlays the rigid projections of the held-out anchors and their tracked positions, for Pace it compares the distance covered by held action with the prediction from its first four steps, and for Composition it draws the generated camera path of route next to the path chained from single-action strides. final pair shows HY-World 1.5 on the same route before and after fine-tuning (Sec. 6). 47 Evidence for Tab. 1 Tab. 1 summarizes the benchmarks closest to StrideWorld, and the evidence behind every cell is listed below with its source sections. The 3D-test column records diagnostics of scene consistency rather than common protocol on held-out points, and human validation denotes reported comparison whose scope differs across studies. Benchmarks made public after September 15, 2026 are concurrent work. Of these, Orbia [32] appears in Tab. 1 and is marked . StreamEval [43], also concurrent, scores whether each online control produces the requested scene operation in streaming generation and is not listed in the table. WorldRoamBench [55] was first released as WorldOdysseyBench in June 2026. WorldScore [9]: Camera and text specifications drive sequential next-scene generation (Sec. 3.1). The camera error fits translation scale, and 3D consistency is dense reprojection error after joint refinement of depth and pose rather than test on points held out from the fit (Sec. 3.3, Supp. C.1C.2). No held-action pace test is reported, and comparisons between metrics and human judgments are given in Supp. D. WorldMark [56]: Key, camera, and text adapters are evaluated for direction, latency, and the speed stability of held commands from optical flow (Secs. 3.1.1, 3.4), and the action suite includes open sequences and round trips (Sec. 3.3). Global Memory uses cross-frame geometry from VGGT-Ω (Sec. 3.1.2), which makes it 3D test rather than only an appearance proxy. Forty raters assess selected metrics, excluding Global Memory (Sec. 4.3). iWorld-Bench [11]: Three native interfaces are tested on action tasks, camera following, and cyclic memory tasks (Sec. 3.2). ViPE trajectories support comparisons of direction and with reference trajectories, and the symmetry of images and displacements serves as an indirect proxy for scene consistency (Sec. 3.3). The human study covers visual quality and camera control with 12 raters and 16 tasks per model (Sec. 4.2.1, App. E.1) and does not validate rigidity specifically. WBench [61]: Key, camera, and text models are evaluated by comparing MegaSaM trajectories with references derived from the actions, together with the consistency of repeated actions (Sec. 4, App. C.4.1), which is proxy for pace rather than direct trace of the speed of held key. Navigation includes open paths and loops (App. A.3), and reprojection with DA3 supplies the geometry tests (App. C.5.6). Four hundred raters compare ten aspects at the granularity of model rankings (Sec. 5.4). WorldExam [58]: Camera, action, and text interfaces are evaluated, with camera inputs using their own trajectory as the reference and action and text segments using prescribed directions with magnitude normalization. Open control sequences and revisits through inverse actions are both evaluated (Secs. 3.2, 4.1), and geometry uses cycle reprojection with VGGT-Ω. Human validation concerns the reactivity checklists and not all geometry metrics (Sec. 5.6). WorldRoamBench [55]: shared keyboard vocabulary is adapted to native key, camera, and text models (App. B.1), and direction labels are complemented by adaptive reference trajectories with arc-length alignment (Sec. 3.2, App. E). Open action sequences and revisits are included (Sec. 4.2). Geometry compares reconstructed point clouds of observations and revisits, and crops of engine references additionally support tests of perceptual consistency (Secs. 3.43.5, App. G.2.3). Human verification concerns the physics and subject-memory judgments of VLM (App. L.2). MIND [59]: Key actions are tested at changed action scales (Secs. 3.23.3), with action accuracy measured from ViPE trajectories by Sim(3) alignment and relative pose errors, and generalization across the action space measured by the MSE between generated and reference frames (Sec. 3.5). Image MSE between forward and reverse passes tests revisits as an appearance proxy rather than held-out 3D rigidity. No direct test of speed decay under held command is reported, and human evaluation is mentioned without protocol or an agreement statistic (Sec. 4.3). World Models as Group Actions [51]: Continuous ego-motion increments are probed with identity, inverse, and local composition relations (Secs. 2.1, 3.3). DROID-SLAM recovers the motion states, and robustness is also assessed by comparing full trajectories across stochastic rollouts (App. C.4, C.7), so Poses denotes the recovery of motion states rather than test of scene rigidity. Neither pace test for held commands nor human validation is reported. WorldCycle (CycleBench) [14]: Key and camera models are tested on reversible, closed, repeated, and cascaded cycles (Sec. 4, App. A). RoMa evaluates endpoint closure, mirrored forward and reverse frames, and phase-aligned states of repeated cycles, so the evaluation is not limited to endpoints, and the drift over repeated cycles serves as an indirect pace proxy in image space. Neither 3D rigidity nor human validation is reported. Orbia [32]: Native-interface adapters are evaluated with directional control scores and templates for exploration and revisits (Sec. 3, App. C.1). Geometry uses registered RGB-D, cross-view tests with recovered cameras, and Gaussian rendering of 16 held-out views from 64 context frames (Sec. 4), which holds out views rather than splitting anchors into pose and test sets as StrideWorld does. Twenty raters compare 90 cases across six models and six evaluation tiers (Sec. 5.7), and no pace test for held actions is reported.

sections.title: M Limitations
sections.content: Scope. Strides test consistency with models own first steps and cannot be measured reliably when model moves too little in its first steps (marked ). Anchors cover only surfaces visible in the start view, so large turns that move these surfaces out of view leave the measurable range, and we report scores on recoverable subsets alongside the overall scores. For the same reason, StrideWorld does not evaluate long-horizon exploration or revisits, whose references would have to be reconstructed from the generated frames themselves. All scenes are static and the main test scores planar motion, with pitch evaluated separately (App. A.6, B.3, and E.3). Extending anchor-based and self-referential evaluation to dynamic scenes and full 6-DoF trajectories is natural next step. Measurement. The Rigidity offset measures departure from the true geometry of the start view, so it covers both deformation over time and scene that stays rigid at wrong depth, and the refitting experiments of App. G.3 separate the two. Because the camera is recovered from the same generated frames and tracks that the Rigidity test uses, deforming scene shifts the recovered camera as well, by median of 0.64 strides at 1 of smooth deformation. At deformation comparable to that of the generated videos, this changes the Near decision of 8% to 20% of the counterpart routes while leaving the model ranking unchanged (App. G.4). The Composition score compares where routes end, and the per-step diagnostics complement it along the route. Control settings.
